Introduction
What is Statistics?
Statistics is the branch of science that deals with the collection, organization,presentation, analysis,
interpretation, and drawing conclusions from data.
Statistics helps us make decisions based on data instead of assumptions.
“Statistics” is a word that has been derived from the Latin word ‘Status’ that implies a gathering of
numbers or figures; those address some data of our human interest.
We discover Statistics in regular day to day existence, such as in books or other information papers
or TV or newspapers. Although, in the first place it was utilized by Kings just for gathering data
about states and other data which was required about their people, their number, income of the state
etc. In India, it is felt that it began tracing all the way back to Chandra Gupta Maurya's realm under
Chankya to gather the information of births and deaths. In any case, presently its extension has
expanded. It is presently utilized in practically all fields of human information and abilities like
Business, Commerce, Economics, Social Sciences, Politics, Planning, Medicine and different
sciences, Physical just as natural.
Definitions of Statistics:
i)Webster Definition: The classified facts respecting the condition of the people in a
state—especially those facts which can be stated in numbers or in tables of numbers or in any tabular
or classified arrangement.
ii) Horace Sacrist Definition: By statistics we mean aggregates of facts affected to a marked extent
by multiplicity of causes, numerically expressed, enumerated or estimated according to a
reasonable standard of accuracy, collected in a systematic manner for a predetermined purpose, and
placed in relation to each other.
iii) Croxton and Cowden Definition:Statistics may be defined as the collection, presentation,
analysis, and interpretation of numerical data.
So, from the above definitions we find that the science of statistics also includes the methods of
collecting, organizing, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical facts and decisions are taken
on their basis.
1.2 Importance of Statistics
In the ancient times Statistics was used to collect information relating to population
wealth, military strength etc. Moreover, with the developments in the statistical techniques during
the last few decades, today, Statistics is viewed as a means of sound techniques for their handling
and analysis and drawing valid inferences from them.

Statistics is important from the following point of views:
i) Statistics facilitates several functions apart from summarization.
ii) Statistical methods give tools of comparison
iii) Statistical methods help in planning, controlling, etc.
iv) We can get an idea about the shape, symmetry of the data
v) Statistical methods give systematic methods of data collection and investigation.
vi) By using statistical methods we can save time, money and manpower.
vii) Estimation, prediction is also possible using statistical tools.
1.3 Scope of Statistics
a)Statistics and planning: Statistics are indispensable into planning in the modern age which is
termed as “the age of planning”- may it be in business, economics or government level. The
statistical data relating to production, consumption, prices, income and expenditure and so on and
the advanced statistical techniques handling such data.
b)Statistics and economics: Statistical data and techniques of statistical analysis have to be
immensely useful involving economical problems. Such as wages, price, time series analysis,
demand analysis.
c) Statistics and business: Statistics is an irresponsible tool of production control. Business
executives are relying more and more on statistical techniques for studying the much and desire of
the valued customers.
d)Statistics and industry: In industry statistics is widely used inequality control. In production
engineering to find out whether the product is conforming to the specifications or not. Statistical
tools, such as inspection plan, control chart etc.
e) Statistics and mathematics: Statistics are intimately related; recent advancements in statistical
technique are the outcome of wide applications of mathematics. The interaction of mathematics and
statistics started in the mid seventeenth century with the development of the theory of probability.
f) Statistics and modern science: In medical science the statistical tools for collection, presentation
and analysis of observed facts relating to causes and incidence of diseases and the result of
application of various drugs and medicine are of great importance.
g)Statistics, psychology and education: In education and physiology statistics has found wide
application such as, determining or to determine the reliability and validity to a test, factor analysis
etc.
1.4.2 Collection of Data :- Collection of data is a vital work and should be done carefully. Prior to
gathering the data we need to choose the objective clearly. There are two types of data collection
a)Primary data:- Primary data is a sort of information that is gathered by specialists
straightforwardly from principle sources through interviews, surveys, experiments, etc. Primary data
are normally gathered from the source where the data originally originates from and are viewed as
the most ideal sort of data in research. So primary data implies original data. This might be viewed
as firsthand data. A classical example of primary data is population census results. Primary data is
more reliable than any other type however it is costly and tedious.The data which are originally
collected for the first time for the purpose of survey are called Primary data.
Methods of collecting Primary data :-
i) Direct personal investigation
ii) Indirect investigation
iii) Through correspondent
iv) By mailed questionnaire

b)Secondary data :-Secondary data is the data that has effectively been gathered through primary
sources and made readily available for researchers to use for their own research. It is a kind of data
that has effectively been gathered previously.
Data taken from the sources like office records, reports etc. which are already collected by some
other agency is called secondary data. Secondary data are also called finished data because it is
already collected, may be tabulated, classified etc.
1.1.Data Types
Basic Concepts of Statistics
1.1.1 Attribute
Definition : An attribute is a characteristic or quality that cannot be measured numerically but
can only be identified or classified.
Attributes describe qualities rather than quantities.
Examples : Gender,Blood group,Religion,Marital Status,Nationality.Eye Colour,Literacy etc.

Blood group is an attribute because it is a category, not a measurable value. Attributes are measured
using nominal and ordinal scale.
a) Nominal Scale: Nominal Scale consists of two or more named categories into which the objects
are classified.
For example: i) Classification of students in various divisions of the same standard.
ii) Classification of workers according to skill.
iii) Classification of students according to gender.
b) Ordinal scale: Ordinal Scale of measurement gives numbers to groups of objects using some
quantifiable characteristics. Therefore ordered arrangement of groups is possible in this scale.
For example: i) Groups of students according to grades in examinations , such as fail , second class ,
first class, distinction etc.
ii) Groups using height such as short, medium, tall
iii) Groups of individuals as dull or intelligent
iv) Groups of individuals according to income such as poor, middle class, rich.
Characteristics of Attributes : Non-numerical,Used for classification,Usually expressed in categories
and Cannot be measured with units .
1.1.2. Variable
Definition : A variable is a characteristic that can take different numerical values for different
individuals or objects.
Unlike attributes, variables can be measured.
Examples : Age,Height,Weight.Income,Marks ,Temperature etc.

Qualitative variables are classified on the basis of descriptive characteristics or attributes.

1.1.5.Classification of Data
Classification is a process related to categorization, the process in which ideas and objects are
recognized, differentiated and understood.
After collection of data, the first step is classification. Classification is the
grouping of related facts into classes. Classification of statistical data is comparable to the sorting
operation. For example, when students seek admission in a college they submit applications to the
office. The application forms contain particulars about their performance in the previous
examination, their date of birth, sex, nationality etc. If one is interested in finding out how many
first, second and third class students have joined the college, one may look into each and every form

and note whether it relates to a first, second class student etc. The process with the help of which this
information in a summary form is obtained is called the classification of data.
Objective of classification
The principal objectives of classifying the data are :
i) To condense the mass of data in such a manner that similarities and dissimilarities can be
readily apprehended. Millions of figures can thus be arranged in a few classes having
common features.
ii) To facilitate comparison.
iii) To point out the most significant features of the data at a glance.
iv) To focus on the important information collected.
v) To enable a statistical treatment of the material collected.

i) Raw Data: The unprocessed data in terms of individual observations is called raw data.
ii) Frequency: The number of observations in a class is called frequency.
iii) Class limits: The two numbers assigning the class interval are called as class limits.

1.2.Data Presentation
Data :
The word ‘Data "is frequently used in ordinary conversation. Data is collected in many
aspects of everyday life. For example , the time required by a runner to complete a marathon, the

number of shots on goal during a period of hockey , correct and incorrect answers given by a student
in an examination etc.
a) Collection of Data:It is the first stage of investigation and is regarding collection of data. It is
determined which method of collection is needed in this problem and then data is collected.
b) Organization of Data: It is the second stage. The data are simplified and made comparative and
are classified according to time and place.
c) Presentation of Data: In this third stage, organized data is made simple and attractive. These are
presented in the form of table diagrams and graphs.
d) Analysis of Data:Fourth stage of investigation is analysis. To get correct results, analysis is
necessary. It is often undertaken using Measures of central tendency, Measures of dispersion etc.
e) Interpretation of Data: Interpretation of data is the process of converting analyzed data into
meaningful information to draw valid conclusions and make informed decisions.
It makes data easy to understand and analyze.

Partition values
Partition values are positional measures that divide a sorted data into equal parts,
median, quartiles, deciles, and percentiles are the partition values.
Types of Partition Values
Quartiles (Q): Divide data into 4 equal parts.Q₁ (First/Lower Quartile): Marks the
25th percentile (25% of data lie below). Q₂ (Second Quartile): Marks the 50th
percentile (the Median). The 75th percentile (75 percent of data lie below) is
represented by Q3 (Third/Upper Quartile).
Deciles (D): Divide data into 10 equal parts (D₁ through D₉). Each decile segment
represents 10% of the dataset.
Percentiles (P): Divide data into 100 equal parts (P₁ through P₉₉). Each percentile
represents 1% of the dataset.
Median: A fundamental partition value that divides the data into two equal halves (50
percent above, 50 percent below), equivalent to Q2, D5, and P50,

Measures of Central Tendency
In the previous unit we learned about data collection and Tabulation as well as classification of data.
We may have to investigate this classified data. Quite possibly the most powerful asset to examine is
to calculate a single value which will be the representative of the whole data. This value is called as
average or central tendency.Some important definitions of central tendency or average defined by
various authors as follows
i)An average value is a single value within the range of the data that is used to represent all of the
values in the series. Since an average is somewhere within range of the data, it is also called a
measures of central tendency ----- Croxton & Cowden
ii)The average is sometime described as a number which is typical of the whole group.------ Leabo
iii)Average is an attempt to find one single figure to describe whole of figures.-------Clark
From the above definitions we say that a single value which will be representative of whole data and
around which a large proportion of observations are clustered are called average or measures of
central tendency.
Objectives of Central Tendency
There are two main objectives of central tendency or average
i) To get a single value for the entire data.
ii)To facilitate comparison.
Properties of Central Tendency:
i)It should be simple to understand and easy to calculate.

iii)This is based on all the observations in the data.
iv)It should be applicable for quantitative as well as qualitative data.

Unit 1: Introduction to Software Engineering
Software, in its most general sense, is a set of instructions or programs instructing a
computer to do specific tasks.
Software is more than just a program code. A program is an executable code, which serves
some computational purpose. Software is considered to be a collection of executable
programming code, associated libraries and documentations.
Software Characteristics
Software Characteristics are classified into six major components:

Definition of Software Engineering
The term software engineering is composed of two words,
software and engineering.
Software is more than just a program code. A program is an
executable code, which serves some computational purpose.
Software is considered to be a collection of executable
programming code, associated libraries and documentations.
Software, when made for a specific requirement is called
software product.
Engineering on the other hand, is all about developing products,
using well-defined, scientific principles and methods. So, we can

define
software engineering as an engineering branch associated with
the development of software product using well-defined
scientific principles, methods and procedures. The outcome of
software engineering is an efficient and reliable software
product.
IEEE defines software engineering as:
The application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable
approach to the development, operation and maintenance of
software
1. Evolving Role of Software

Definition
Software is a collection of programs, data, and documents that instruct a computer
to perform specific tasks. Over time, software has become one of the most
important technologies in the world.
Earlier, software was used only for calculations and business records. Today, it is
used in almost every area of life such as education, banking, healthcare,
transportation, entertainment, communication, and scientific research.
Evolution of Software
1. Early Stage (1950–1970)
Software was developed only for specific computers.

Programs were small and simple.
Mostly used for mathematical calculations and scientific work.
Very few people used computers
2. Business Software Era
Companies started using software for payroll, accounting, inventory, and
banking. Databases became popular.
Software helped automate business operations.
3. Personal Computer Era
Personal computers became common.
Office applications such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint were
introduced. Home users started using software for education and
entertainment. 4. Internet Era

Websites became popular.
Email and online communication increased.
Online shopping and online banking started.
Social media applications became common.
5. Modern Era
Mobile applications are widely used.
Cloud computing allows software to run online.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) makes software smarter.
Current Role of Software
Software is used in almost every
field. Education
• Online classes

• Digital libraries
• Learning apps
• Online examinations
Healthcare
• Hospital management
• Patient records
• Medical diagnosis
• Online consultation
Banking
• Internet banking

• Mobile banking
• ATM systems
• Digital payments
Business
• Payroll management • Inventory management • Customer management •
Accounting
Entertainment
• Video streaming
• Music apps
• Online games

•
Transportation
• Online ticket booking
• GPS navigation
• Traffic management •
Flight reservation systems
Government
• Online services
• Digital identity systems

• Tax management
• E-governance
Importance of
Software • Saves time
• Reduces human effort
• Improves accuracy
• Increases productivity •
Stores large amounts of data •
Supports communication •

Automates complex tasks •
Helps in decision making
2. Changing Nature of Software
Definition
The changing nature of software means software technology keeps improving according
to user needs and technological advancements.
Modern software is faster, smarter, more secure, and available on different
devices. Reasons for Change
• New technologies
• Customer requirements

• Internet growth
• Mobile devices
• Cloud computing
• Artificial Intelligence
• Cybersecurity needs
Characteristics of Modern
Software 1. Web Applications
Software runs through internet
browsers. Examples:
• Gmail

• Google Docs
• Amazon
Advantages
• No installation required
• Accessible from anywhere
• Easy updates
2. Mobile Applications
Applications designed for smartphones and tablets.
Examples

• WhatsApp
• Instagram
• Paytm
Features
• Portable
• Easy to use
• Fast communication
3. Cloud Computing
Software and data are stored on remote

servers.
Examples
• Google Drive
• Dropbox
• Microsoft OneDrive
Advantages
• Access from anywhere
• Automatic backup
• Low maintenance

4. Artificial Intelligence
AI allows software to think and
learn. Examples
• Chatbots
• Voice assistants
• Recommendation systems
Benefits
• Automation

• Better decision making
• Personalized services
5. Internet of Things (IoT)
Physical devices communicate
through software.
Examples
• Smart TV
• Smart Watch

• Smart Home
• Smart Car
6. Cyber Security
Software now includes strong security
features.
Examples
• Password protection

• Encryption
• Firewalls
• Multi-factor authentication
Features of Modern
Software • User friendly
• Intelligent
• Secure
• Scalable

• Fast
• Cloud-enabled
• Mobile compatible
• Easy to maintain
Evolving Role and Changing Nature of Software
Software has evolved from simple programs used for basic calculations into
an essential part of almost every field.
1. From standalone programs to complex systems: Earlier, software mainly
performed specific tasks. Today, it includes large, interconnected systems
such as cloud platforms, operating systems, and enterprise applications.

2. Integration into everyday life: Software is now used in banking,
healthcare, education, transportation, communication, entertainment,
and many other areas.
3. Web and mobile applications: The growth of the Internet and
smartphones has changed software from desktop-based applications to
web-based and mobile applications that can be accessed anywhere.
4. Cloud and AI-based software: Modern software increasingly
uses cloud computing, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and
data analytics to provide intelligent and scalable service.

5. Changing nature of software: Software is no longer developed
once and left unchanged. It is continuously updated, maintained,
secured, and improved to meet changing user needs and
technological requirements.
Thus, software has changed from a simple supporting tool into a
critical technology that drives businesses, services, and modern
society.
Software engineering – A layered technology
Software engineering is a fully layered technology. To develop software,
we need to go from one layer to another. All the layers are connected
and each layer demands the fulfillment of the previous layer.

Layered technology is divided into four parts:
1. A quality focus
It defines the continuous process improvement principles of software. It
provides integrity that means providing security to the software so that
data can be accessed by only an authorized person, no outsider can
access the data. It also focuses on maintainability and usability. It
ensures
∙ Reliable software
∙ Secure
∙ Correct output

∙ High performance
Customer satisfaction
2. Process
It is the foundation or base layer of software engineering. It is key that binds all the
layers together which enables the development of software before the deadline or on
time. Process defines a framework that must be established for the effective delivery of
software engineering technology. The software process covers all the activities, actions,
and tasks required to be carried out for software development.
Purpose
∙ Organize work

∙ Reduce errors
∙ Improve quality
∙ Complete projects on time
3. Method
During the process of software development the answers to all “how-to-do”
questions are given by method. It has the information of all the tasks which includes
communication, requirement analysis, design modelling, program construction,
testing, and support.
They include
∙ Requirement analysis

∙ Software design
∙ Coding
∙ Testing
∙ Maintenance
4. Tools
Software engineering tools provide a self-operating system for processes and methods.
Tools are integrated which means information created by one tool can be used by
another.
Tools help developers perform tasks efficiently.
Examples

∙ Visual Studio
∙ Eclipse
∙ IntelliJ IDEA
∙ Git
∙ Jenkins
∙ Selenium
Benefits
∙ Faster development
∙ Better testing
∙ Improved productivity

Advantages of Layered
Technology ∙ Better software
quality
∙ Eases project management ∙
Improves teamwork
∙ Reduces development time ∙
Increases customer satisfaction
A process framework
A Software Process Framework is a structured approach that defines the steps,
tasks, and activities involved in software development. This framework serves as a
foundation for software engineering

Software Process Framework Activities
The five generic process framework activities useful in developing several projects
are given below:

1. Communication
Definition: Communication involves gathering requirements from customers and
stakeholders to determine the system's objectives and the software's
requirements. Activities:
∙ Requirement Gathering: Engaging with consumers and stakeholders through meetings,
interviews, and surveys to understand their needs and expectations.
∙ Objective Setting: Clearly defining what the system should achieve based on the
gathered requirements.
Explanation: Effective communication is essential to understand what the users need from
the software. This phase ensures that all stakeholders are on the same page regarding the
goals and requirements of the system.

2. Planning
Definition: Planning involves establishing an engineering work plan, describing technical
risks, listing resource requirements, and defining a work schedule.
Activities:
∙ Work Plan: Creating a detailed plan that outlines the tasks and activities needed to
develop the software.
∙ Risk Assessment: Identifying potential technical risks and planning how to mitigate
them.
∙ Resource Allocation: Determining the resources (time, personnel, tools) required for
the project.
∙ Schedule Definition: Setting a timeline for completing different phases of the project.

Explanation: Planning helps in organizing the project and setting clear expectations. It
ensures that the development team has a roadmap to follow and that potential challenges
are anticipated and managed.
Modeling
Definition: Modeling involves creating architectural models and designs to better
understand the problem and work towards the best solution.
Activities:
∙ Analysis of Requirements: Breaking down the gathered requirements to understand
what the system needs to do.
∙ Design: Creating architectural and detailed designs that outline how the software will be
structured and how it will function.

Explanation: Modeling translates requirements into a visual and structured representation
of the system. It helps in identifying the best design approach and serves as a blueprint for
development.
4. Construction
Definition: Construction involves creating code, testing the system, fixing bugs, and
confirming that all criteria are met.
Activities:
∙ Code Generation: Writing the actual code based on the design models. ∙ Testing: Running
tests to ensure the software works as intended, identifying and fixing bugs.
Explanation: This phase is where the actual software is built. Testing is crucial to ensure
that the code is error-free and that the software meets all specified requirements.

5. Deployment
Definition: Deployment involves presenting the completed or partially completed
product to customers for evaluation and feedback, then making necessary
modifications based on their input.
Activities:
∙ Product Release: Delivering the software to users, either as a full release or in
stages.
∙ Feedback Collection: Gathering feedback from users about their experience with
the software.
∙ Product Improvement: Making changes and improvements based on user feedback
to enhance the product.

Umbrella Activities
Umbrella Activities that take place during a software development process for improved project
management and tracking.
1. Software project tracking and control: This is an activity in which the team can assess
progress and take corrective action to maintain the schedule. Take action to keep the project
on time by comparing the project's progress against the plan.
2. Risk management: The risks that may affect project outcomes or quality can be analyzed.
Analyze potential risks that may have an impact on the software product's quality and
outcome.
3. Software quality assurance: These are activities required to maintain software quality.

Perform actions to ensure the product's quality.
4. Formal technical reviews: It is required to assess engineering work products to uncover
and remove errors before they propagate to the next activity. At each level of the process,
errors are evaluated and fixed.
5. Software configuration management: Managing of configuration process when any
change in the software occurs.
6. Work product preparation and production: The activities to create models, documents,
logs, forms, and lists are carried out.
7. Reusability management: It defines criteria for work product reuse. Reusable work
items should be backed up, and reusable software components should be achieved. 8.
Measurement: In this activity, the process can be defined and collected. Also, project

and product measures are used to assist the software team in delivering the required
software.
Process models
Software development life cycle
Software development life cycle (SDLC) is a structured process that is used to
design, develop, and test good-quality software. SDLC, or software development life
cycle, is a methodology that defines the entire procedure of software development
step-by-step. The goal of the SDLC life cycle model is to deliver high-quality,
maintainable software that meets the user’s requirements. SDLC in software
engineering models outlines the plan for each stage so that each stage of the
software development model can perform its task efficiently to deliver the software
at a low cost within a given time frame that meets user’s requirements.

The SDLC Model
involves six phases
or stages while
developing any
software.
Requirements analysis
phase
Requirements analysis

and specification phase is very important in the successful development of a
software. If the customer requirements are not analysed properly, the chances of
project failure or amount of rework on project becomes very high. Therefore, the
project startup without proper requirements analysis and documentation is
considered as a major mistake.
It also increases the burden on developer to reflect/implement the changes multiple
times. Such iterations increase the cost incurred in the overall project and also leads
to customer dissatisfaction.
The importance of requirements understanding and documentation is independent of
the type of project i.e., internal or contract based. The documentation generated
after successful analysis and specification is called Software Requirement
Specification (SRS) document. This document not only helps in getting a clear

understanding about product requirements, but also helps in carrying out different
activities of later phases.
Design phase
Design is a meaningful engineering representation of something that is to be built. It can
be traced to a customer’s requirements and at the same time assessed for quality
against a set of predefined criteria for “good” design. In the software engineering
context, design focuses on four major areas of concern – data, architecture, interfaces
and components.
Software design process is an iterative process through which requirements document
(SRS) is transformed to design document.
Implementation and unit testing phase
In this phase, actual code is developed using a programming language. As soon as the

code is developed, each unit or component in it is tested individually. Such testing is
called unit testing. It ensures that maximum errors are detected and entire code is
tested by following certain paths in the control structure
Testing phase
Testing is a major activity for software development and its main function is to detect bugs
or errors that occur while executing a software. During the phases like requirement
analysis and system design, the output results in the form of textual documents whereas,
for the coding phase, the output is a computer program. Hence, testing not only detect
errors during
Deployment phase
This forms the final phase of the software development process where the software is
usually delivered to the end users for its effective implementation. Later, feedback is

collected from the users and if, the software fails to meet the users requirements, it is
modified. Hence, the important activities involved in this phase are:- ∙ Perfect delivery
∙ Support and
∙ Feedbacks.
Maintenance phase
Software maintenance refers to the changes which are performed once the software is
delivered to users. Maintenance activity is compulsory for each type of product and cannot
be avoided. Generally, products require maintenance activity due to its heavy usage. But,
software need maintenance in order to improve features, correct errors. It is an essential
activity adopted by large number of organization because of the misuse of hardware.
Top 8 Software Development Models

1. Waterfall Model
2. Incremental Model
3. Agile Model
4. V-Model
5. RAD Model
6. Iterative Model
7. Spiral Model
8. Prototype model
Waterfall Model
The Waterfall Model was the first Process Model to be
introduced. It is also referred to as a linear-sequential life cycle

model.
It is very simple to understand and use.
In a waterfall model, each phase must be completed before the
next phase can begin and there is no overlapping in the phases.
The Waterfall model is the earliest SDLC approach that was used
for software development.
Waterfall approach to be used widely in Software Engineering to
ensure success of the project.
In "The Waterfall" approach, the whole process of software
development is divided into separate phases.
In this Waterfall model, typically, the outcome of one phase acts
as the input for the next phase sequentially.

Requirement Gathering and analysis −The first stage focuses on clearly
understanding and documenting the customer’s needs.
Requirement Gathering and Analysis: Customer requirements are collected and
carefully examined to remove errors, confusion, and inconsistencies.
Requirement Specification: The approved requirements are documented in the
Software Requirement Specification (SRS), which serves as a formal agreement
between the customer and the development team.
System Design − The requirement specifications from first phase are studied in this
phase and the system design is prepared. This system design helps in specifying
hardware and system requirements and helps in defining the overall system
architecture. The requirements specified in the SRS are converted into a system
design that can be implemented in code.

High-Level Design (HLD): Defines the overall system architecture, major
components, and their interactions.
Low-Level Design (LLD): Provides detailed design of each component, including logic
and data flow, to guide developers during coding.
All designs are documented in the Software Design Document (SDD).
Development − This phase involves converting the design into actual working
software. Developers write source code based on the design documents.
Suitable programming languages and tools are used.
Unit testing is performed to verify that each module works correctly on its own.
Testing: After unit testing, software modules are integrated and integration testing is
performed. Once integration is complete, system testing is carried out to verify the entire
system.

•Final release
Step 6: Create the Schedule
Scheduling tools may include:
•Gantt charts
•Network diagrams
•Critical Path Method
•PERT
•Agile release plans

Agile Planning
Agile planning is an iterative approach in which planning is performed continuously as the project evolves.
Unlike detailed long-term planning, Agile generally emphasizes short-term, adaptive planning.
Main characteristics
•Iterative development
•Incremental delivery
•Frequent customer feedback
•Continuous reprioritization
•Flexible requirements
•Short development cycles
•Planning at multiple levels

Agile Planning Levels
Product Vision
Describes the overall purpose of the product.
Example:
Product Roadmap
Shows major product goals and expected releases.
Example:
•Release 1: User registration
•Release 2: Course management
•Release 3: Online assessments
•Release 4: Analytics
Build an online learning platform that enables students to access courses, assignments, and assessments.
Release Planning
Determines which features are targeted for a particular release.
Iteration/Sprint Planning
Determines the work to be completed during the next iteration.
Daily Planning
Teams coordinate work during daily meetings.
Backlog Refinement
User stories are:
•Clarified
•Estimated
•Prioritized
•Split into smaller stories when necessary

User Stories
A user story describes functionality from the user's perspective.
Common format:
As a [type of user],
Iwant [functionality],
so that [benefit].
Example:
As a customer, I want to reset my password so that I can regain access to my account.
User stories are typically accompanied by acceptance criteria defining when the story is considered complete.
Product Backlog
The product backlog is a prioritized list of work required for the product.
It can contain:
•User stories
•Features
•Bugs
•Technical work
•Improvements
•Research tasks
Items near the top are generally more important and better understood than lower-priority items.

Agile Estimation
Agile teams commonly estimate work using relative size rather than attempting to predict exact hours for
every task.
Common units include:
•Story points
•Ideal days
•T-shirt sizes
Story Points
Story points represent relative effort considering factors such as:
•Complexity
•Amount of work
•Uncertainty
•Technical difficulty
Example:
Story Story
Points
Login 2
Profile management 3
Payment integration 8
Recommendation engine 13

Estimation Techniques
Software estimation attempts to determine:
•Effort
•Development time
•Cost
•Resources
Estimation is difficult because software projects contain uncertainty.
Expert Judgment
Experienced developers/managers estimate the required effort based on their
knowledge.
Advantages
•Fast
•Simple
•Useful when historical data is limited
Disadvantages
•Subjective
•Can be affected by bias
•Different experts may produce different estimates

Estimation by Analogy
The current project is compared with similar completed projects.
Example:
Previous project:
•10,000 lines of code
•12 person-months
New project appears approximately 25% larger.
Estimated effort might be around:
12 × 1.25 = 15 person-months
Advantages
•Uses real historical experience
•Easy to understand
Disadvantages
•Requires sufficiently similar historical projects
•Differences between projects can make estimates inaccurate

Top-Down Estimation
The project is estimated as a whole first, and the total estimate is then divided among components.
Example:
Total estimated effort = 100 person-months
Then:
•Requirements = 10%
•Design = 15%
•Coding = 40%
•Testing = 25%
•Deployment = 10%
Advantages
•Quick
•Useful in early project stages
Disadvantages
•Individual tasks may be underestimated.
•Details may be overlooked.

Bottom-Up Estimation
The project is divided into smaller tasks, each task is estimated, and the estimates are
added.
Example:
Login 2 days
Registration 3 days
Payment 5 days
Reporting 4 days
Testing 6 days
----------------------------
Total 20 days
Advantages
•Detailed
•Often more accurate when requirements are understood
•Makes assumptions visible
Disadvantages
•Time-consuming
•Difficult early in the project
•Small estimation errors can accumulate

Three-Point Estimation
Three estimates are produced:
•Optimistic (O): best-case estimate
•Most likely (M): normal expected estimate
•Pessimistic (P): worst reasonable estimate
A commonly used PERT-style expected estimate is:
E=O+4M+P6
Example
Suppose:
•O = 4 days
•M = 6 days
•P = 10 days

Three-point Estimation — Example
Suppose login module estimates are: O = 2 days, M = 4 days, P = 8 days.
Expected effort = (2 + 4×4 + 8) / 6 = 26/6 ≈ 4.33 days.
This method considers uncertainty rather than relying on one number.
Add estimates for all major work packages to obtain a project-level estimate.

Planning Poker
Planning Poker is an Agile estimation technique.
Process
1.Product owner explains a user story.
2.Team discusses the requirements.
3.Each team member privately selects an estimate.
4.Everyone reveals the estimate simultaneously.
5.High and low estimates are discussed.
6.The team estimates again.
7.The process continues until a reasonable consensus is reached.
Typical cards use values such as:
1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21
Benefits
Encourages team participation
Reduces influence from dominant individuals
Encourages discussion
Makes uncertainty visible
These values often follow a Fibonacci-like sequence because uncertainty increases as work becomes larger.

Function Point Estimation
Function Point Analysis (FPA) estimates software size based on functionality delivered to users rather than directly
counting lines of code.
Common function types include:
•External Inputs (EI)
•External Outputs (EO)
•External Inquiries (EQ)
•Internal Logical Files (ILF)
•External Interface Files (EIF)
A simplified process is:
1.Identify functions.
2.Classify their complexity.
3.Assign weights.
4.Calculate unadjusted function points.
5.Apply adjustment factors if the chosen FPA method requires them.
Function points can then be related to historical productivity data to estimate effort.
Advantages
•Can be used before implementation.
•Independent of a specific programming language.
•Focuses on user-visible functionality.
Disadvantages
•Requires trained estimators.
•Classification can be subjective.
•More difficult for some modern systems.

LOC-Based Estimation
LOC = Lines of Code
Effort is estimated using expected source-code size and historical productivity.
For example:
If productivity is:
500 LOC/person-month
and estimated size is:
5,000 LOC
then:
Effort=5000500=10 person-months
Problems with LOC
•Difficult to estimate LOC early.
•Different programming languages produce different amounts of code.
•More code does not necessarily mean more functionality.
•Encouraging more LOC can create undesirable incentives.

9. Estimation Techniques
▪ Expert judgment: experienced people estimate effort based on similar work.
▪ Analogous estimation: compare with a previous similar project.
▪ Top-down estimation: estimate the whole project, then distribute effort.
▪ Bottom-up estimation: estimate individual tasks/work packages and add them.
▪ Three-point estimation: optimistic (O), most likely (M), pessimistic (P). Expected estimate = (O + 4M
+ P) / 6.
▪ Function Point / Use Case Point methods estimate based on system functionality.

Prioritize work by business value and risk.

pages.text:
Machine Learning is a technique that allows computers to learn from data and make
decisions without explicit programming. It works by identifying patterns in data and
using them to make predictions. It is used in areas such as: Image Recognition,
Speech Processing, Language Translation and Recommender Systems.
Real-World Example
If you frequently watch action movies on Netflix, Machine Learning can identify this
preference and suggest more action movies or similar shows. Similarly, shopping
apps can use your searches, views and purchases to suggest products you may be
interested in. These personalized recommendations help users discover relevant
content and products more easily.
Need for Machine Learning
Machine Learning is needed for problems where traditional programming is difficult
to scale or requires too many manually defined rules. It can learn patterns from data,
automate tasks and make useful predictions.
1. Solving Complex Problems
ML can handle tasks that are difficult to solve with fixed rules by learning patterns
from data.
Examples:
• Image and speech recognition
• Language translation and medical diagnosis
2. Handling Large Amounts of Data
ML can analyze large datasets to identify patterns, detect anomalies and generate
predictions.
Examples:
• Fraud detection in financial transactions
• Traffic and demand prediction
3. Automating Tasks

ML can automate repetitive tasks, reducing manual effort and improving efficiency.
Examples:
• Spam email detection
• Chatbots for customer support
• Invoice and document processing
4. Personalizing User Experiences
ML analyzes user behavior and preferences to provide personalized recommendations
and content.
Examples:
• Music apps recommending songs based on listening habits
• Shopping apps suggesting products based on searches and purchases
How Machines Learn from Data
Machine Learning uses data to learn patterns and build models that can make
predictions or decisions on new data. The basic process involves the following steps:
1. Data: Machine Learning starts with data such as text, images, numbers or other
information. The quality and relevance of the data are important for effective
2. learning.
Algorithm: An ML algorithm is selected based on the task, such as classification,
regression or clustering.
3. 4. Training: The algorithm learns patterns from the training data and uses them to
build a machine learning model.
Prediction: The trained model applies the learned patterns to new data and
5. produces predictions or results.
Evaluation: The model is tested on unseen data to measure its performance and
ability to generalize to real-world data.
Data is the foundation of machine learning because models learn patterns and make
predictions from it. Good quality and diverse data help improve accuracy,
performance and real-world results.
Applications
• Healthcare: Disease diagnosis, outcome prediction and treatment support
• Finance: Fraud detection, credit risk assessment and trading analysis
• E-commerce: Product recommendations, demand forecasting and customer
behavior analysis
• Transportation: Route optimization, autonomous driving and predictive
maintenance
• Media: Content recommendations, speech recognition and image recognition

• Manufacturing: Defect detection, equipment monitoring and failure prediction
Challenges
• Data Quality and Bias: Poor-quality or biased data can lead to inaccurate or
unfair predictions, so data must be carefully collected and monitored.
• Overfitting and Generalization: A model may perform well on training data but
poorly on new data, making it important to ensure that it generalizes well.
• Privacy: ML systems may process sensitive or personal data, creating privacy and
security risks.
• Explainability: Complex models can be difficult to understand, making it harder
to explain their predictions and decisions.
• Deployment and Resources: ML models can require significant computational
resources and ongoing monitoring and maintenance after deployment.
Types of Machine Learning
• Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that focuses on
building algorithms and models that enable computers to learn from data and improve
with experience without explicit programming for every task. In simple words,
Machine Learning teaches systems to learn patterns and make decisions like humans
by analyzing and learning from data.
There are several types of machine learning, each with special characteristics and
applications. Some of the main types of machine learning algorithms are as follows:
1. Supervised Machine Learning
2. Unsupervised Machine Learning
3. Reinforcement Learning
Additionally, there is a more specific category called Semi-Supervised Learning and
Self-Supervised Learning, which combines elements of both supervised and
unsupervised learning

Types of Machine Learning
1. Supervised Machine Learning
Supervised learning is defined as when a model gets trained on a "Labeled Dataset".
Labelled datasets have both input and output parameters. In Supervised Learning
algorithms learn to map points between inputs and correct outputs. It has both
training and validation datasets labelled.
Supervised Learning

Example: If you train a model using labeled images of cats and dogs, it learns the
features of each. When shown a new image, it predicts whether it’s a cat or a dog.
There are two main categories of supervised learning that are mentioned below:
1. Classification
Classification predicts categorical outputs, meaning it assigns data into predefined
classes like spam/non-spam emails or disease risk categories. These algorithms learn
to map input features to discrete labels. Here are some classification algorithms:
• Logistic Regression
• Decision Tree
• Random Forest
• K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
• Naive Bayes
• Support Vector Machine
2. Regression
Regression, predicts continuous values, such as house prices or product sales. It
learns the relationship between input features and a numerical target variable. Here
are some regression algorithms:
• Linear Regression

• Polynomial Regression
• Ridge Regression
• Lasso Regression
• Decision tree
• Random Forest
Where to Use Supervised Learning
• When you have labeled data and want to predict outcomes.
• Ideal for classification (like spam detection) or regression tasks (like price
forecasting).
• Best used in domains where historical data with outcomes is already available.
Applications
Supervised learning is used in a wide variety of applications, including:
• Image, speech and text processing: For tasks like image classification, speech
recognition and sentiment analysis.
• Predictive analytics: To forecast sales, customer churn, stock prices and weather
conditions.
• Recommendation and personalization: Powering systems that suggest
products, movies or content.
• Healthcare and finance: Used for medical diagnosis, fraud detection and credit
scoring.
• Automation and control: In autonomous vehicles, manufacturing quality checks
and gaming AI.
2. Unsupervised Machine Learning
Unsupervised Learning works with unlabeled data, meaning there are no predefined
outputs. The algorithm finds hidden patterns, groups or relationships within the data
on its own. It’s mainly used for clustering, dimensionality reduction and data
visualization.

Unsupervised Machine Learning
Example: If you have customer data without labels, the algorithm can group similar
customers based on purchase behavior useful for segmentation and marketing.
There are two main categories of unsupervised learning that are mentioned below:
1. Clustering
Clustering is the process of grouping data points into clusters based on their
similarity. This technique is useful for identifying patterns and relationships in data
without the need for labeled examples. Common techniques include:
• K-Means
• DBSCAN
• Mean-shift
2. Dimensionality Reduction Techniques
Dimensionality reduction helps reduce the number of features while preserving
important information. Common techniques include:
• Principal Component Analysis
• Independent Component Analysis

3. Association Rule Learning
Association rule learning is a technique for discovering relationships between items
in a dataset. It identifies rules that indicate the presence of one item implies the
presence of another item with a specific probability. Common techniques include:
• Apriori
• FP-growth
• Eclat
Where to Use Unsupervised Learning
• When data is unlabeled or unstructured.
• Useful for exploratory analysis, clustering or feature extraction.
• Common in marketing, recommendation systems and fraud detection where
patterns matter more than labels.
Applications of Unsupervised Learning
Here are some common applications of unsupervised learning:
• Clustering and segmentation: Group similar data points, customers or images.
• Anomaly detection: Spot unusual patterns or outliers in data.
• Dimensionality reduction: Simplify large datasets while retaining key
information.
• Recommendation and marketing: Identify user preferences and improve
product suggestions.
• Data preprocessing and analysis: Clean data, detect patterns and support
exploratory data analysis (EDA).
3. Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning trains an agent to make a sequence of decisions through trial
and error. The agent interacts with the environment, receives feedback in the form of
rewards or penalties and learns optimal actions over time.
Reinforcement Machine Learning

Example: An AI agent learning to play chess gets positive feedback for good moves
and negative for poor ones. Over time, it learns strategies to win more often.
Here are some of most common reinforcement learning algorithms:
• Q-learning: Learns the best action for each state based on expected rewards.
• SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action): Similar to Q-learning but
updates values for the action actually taken.
• Deep Q-learning: Uses neural networks to handle complex state-action
relationships
Types of Reinforcement Learning
• Positive Reinforcement: Rewards desired behavior (e.g., giving points for
correct answers).
• Negative Reinforcement: Removes negative outcomes to encourage good
actions (e.g., turning off a buzzer after the right move).
Where to Use Reinforcement Learning
• When you need an agent to learn by interacting with an environment.
• Best for decision-making or optimization tasks involving trial and feedback
loops.
• Used when long-term performance or adaptive behavior is more important than
immediate accuracy.
Applications of Reinforcement Learning
Here are some applications of reinforcement learning:
• Gaming and simulation: Teaching agents or NPCs to play and adapt
intelligently.
• Robotics and automation: Enabling robots to perform tasks autonomously.
• Autonomous vehicles: Helping self-driving cars make real-time decisions.
• Healthcare and finance: Optimizing treatment plans, trading and resource
allocation.
• Recommendation and personalization: Improving user experience through
adaptive suggestions.
• Industrial and energy management: Optimizing control systems and energy
use.

Machine learning algorithms
Decision tree
A decision tree is a supervised learning algorithm used for classification and predictive
modelling tasks. It resembles a flowchart, starting with a root node that asks a specific
question about the data. Based on the answer, the data is directed down different
branches to subsequent internal nodes, which ask further questions and guide the data to
subsequent branches. This process continues until the data reaches an end node, a leaf
node, where no further branching occurs.
Decision tree algorithms are popular in machine learning because they can handle
complex datasets with ease and simplicity. The algorithm's structure makes
understanding and interpreting the decision-making process straightforward. Decision
trees enable us to classify or predict outcomes based on the data's characteristics by
asking questions and following the corresponding branches.
This simplicity and interpretability make decision trees valuable for various machine
learning applications, especially when dealing with complex datasets.
Random forest
A random forest algorithm is an ensemble of decision trees used for classification and
predictive modelling. Instead of relying on a single decision tree, a random forest
combines the predictions from multiple decision trees to make more accurate
predictions.
In a random forest, numerous decision tree algorithms (sometimes hundreds or even
thousands) are individually trained using different random samples from the training

dataset. This sampling method is called "bagging." Each decision tree is trained
independently on its respective random sample.
Once trained, the random forest feeds the same data into each decision tree. Each tree
produces a prediction, and the random forest tallies the results. The most common
prediction among all the decision trees is then selected as the final prediction for the
dataset.
Random forests address a common " overfitting " issue with individual decision trees.
Overfitting happens when a decision tree becomes too closely aligned with its training
data, making it less accurate when presented with new data.
Naive Bayes
Naive Bayes is a set of supervised learning algorithms used to create predictive models
for binary or multi-classification tasks. It is based on Bayes' Theorem and operates on
conditional probabilities, which estimate the likelihood of a classification based on the
combined factors while assuming independence between them.
Let's consider a program that identifies plants using a Naive Bayes algorithm. The
algorithm considers specific factors such as perceived size, colour, and shape to
categorise images of plants. Although each factor is considered independently, the
algorithm combines them to assess the probability of an object being a particular plant.
Naive Bayes leverages the assumption of independence among the factors, simplifying
the calculations and allowing the algorithm to work efficiently with large datasets. It is
particularly well-suited for tasks like document classification, email spam filtering,
sentiment analysis, and many other applications where the factors can be considered
separately but still contribute to the overall classification.

Support vector machine (SVM)
A support vector machine (SVM) is a supervised learning algorithm commonly used for
classification and predictive modelling tasks. SVM algorithms are popular because they
are reliable and can work well even with a small amount of data. SVM algorithms work
by creating a decision boundary called a "hyperplane." In two-dimensional space, this
hyperplane is like a line that separates two sets of labelled data.
SVM aims to find the best possible decision boundary by maximising the margin
between the two labelled data sets. It looks for the widest gap or space between the
classes. Any new data point on either side of this decision boundary is classified based
on the labels in the training dataset.
It's important to note that hyperplanes can take on different shapes when plotted in
three-dimensional space, allowing SVM to handle more complex patterns and
relationships in the data.

Unit III — AI Techniques for Software Testing
1. Why AI in Software Testing
Software applications today are larger, more frequently updated, and tested across more devices and
browsers than ever before. Purely manual and traditionally-scripted automated testing struggles to keep
pace with this scale of change. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are increasingly used to
make testing faster, more adaptive, and less dependent on constant manual upkeep.
1.1 Limitations of Traditional Testing
Before looking at what AI brings to testing, it helps to understand the pain points of conventional automated
testing that AI is designed to solve:
● Manual test creation and maintenance: Test cases are written by hand and must be individually
updated whenever the application changes.
● Fragile locators: Automation scripts typically refer to UI elements by a fixed ID, name, or XPath. Even a
small UI redesign can break dozens of scripts at once.
● Time-consuming regression cycles: Large regression suites (sometimes thousands of test cases) take
hours to execute and review, slowing down releases.
● Flaky tests: Some tests fail intermittently for reasons unrelated to real bugs (timing issues, network
delays), and teams waste time investigating false alarms.
● Coverage limited by human capacity: The number and variety of test cases a team can design by hand is
limited by available time and tester experience.
AI-based testing tools directly target each of these limitations, using machine learning models and natural
language processing to make test creation, execution and maintenance considerably more intelligent and
self-sufficient.
1.2 Five Key Reasons to Use AI in Testing
i. Handles Large Test Case Volume
Modern applications can require thousands of regression test cases. Running every test on every build is
often impractical within release timelines. AI models can analyze code changes, historical defect patterns
and test outcomes to intelligently select and prioritize the subset of tests most likely to catch a defect,
instead of running the full suite blindly every time.
Example: A banking application maintains a regression suite of 10,000 test cases. Instead of executing
all of them on every build (which could take many hours), an AI engine analyses which modules changed
and which tests historically catch defects in those modules, then prioritizes and runs the top 500 highest-
risk tests first — giving fast feedback without sacrificing coverage of what matters most.
ii. Adapts to Frequent UI Changes
User interfaces change often — buttons are redesigned, elements are repositioned, and IDs or class names
are regenerated by frameworks. Traditional scripts that rely on a single fixed locator break the moment any
of this changes. AI-based tools instead learn multiple attributes of an element (its text, approximate
position, style, and surrounding context) so they can still recognize it even if one attribute changes.

Example: A "Submit" button's HTML ID changes from #submitBtn to #btn_submit_2024 after a front-end
redesign. A traditional script that hard-codes the old ID immediately fails with an "Element not found"
error. An AI-based tool, however, recognizes the same button by its visible label, its position on the page,
and its visual styling, and continues clicking it correctly without any script changes.
iii. Reduces Automation Maintenance
A large fraction of a test automation team's time is typically spent not writing new tests, but repairing
existing ones after every UI or workflow change. Because AI-based locators adapt automatically (this is often
called "self-healing"), the number of broken scripts after a release drops sharply, freeing testers to focus on
designing new test scenarios rather than patching old ones.
Example: After a UI revamp that would traditionally require a team to manually inspect and rewrite
around 200 Selenium scripts, an AI-based self-healing framework automatically updates the affected
locators itself and simply logs a maintenance report — cutting days of rework down to a quick review of
the log.
iv. Reduces Flaky Scripts
A 'flaky' test is one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any change to the underlying
application — usually because of environment issues like network latency, animation timing, or test-data
conflicts. AI models can learn the difference between a failure pattern caused by a genuine defect and one
caused by an unstable environment, and can suppress or flag the latter instead of reporting it as a bug.
Example: An AI-driven test platform observes that a particular checkout test fails only when the test
environment's network response time exceeds two seconds, and never fails otherwise. It learns this is an
environmental issue, not a real defect, and stops flagging it as a failing test — saving the team from
investigating a false alarm on every run.
v. Improves Speed, Accuracy and Coverage
Because AI systems can execute and analyze large numbers of test combinations in parallel, and can
compare visual output pixel-by-pixel far more consistently than a human reviewer, they improve both the
thoroughness and the reliability of testing — surfacing subtle visual or functional defects that might
otherwise be missed under time pressure.
Example: A visual-AI tool compares thousands of screenshots of a website across different browsers and
screen sizes within minutes, flagging a 2-pixel misalignment in a checkout button on Safari that a human
tester manually reviewing screens might easily miss.

This self-healing capability is the single biggest reason AI-based tools cut automation maintenance effort so

1.4 Popular AI-Powered Testing Tools
A number of commercial and open-source tools now embed AI/ML techniques into their testing workflow. A
few widely used examples:
● Testim: Uses AI to create stable, self-healing locators for web test automation, reducing script breakage
after UI changes.
● Applitools: A Visual AI platform that performs pixel-level UI comparisons to detect visual regressions
that functional tests would miss.
● mabl: A low-code AI testing platform with built-in auto-healing, and analytics that highlight likely causes
of failure.
● Functionize: Uses ML to author, execute and self-heal tests at scale across large web applications.
● Test.ai (part of Tricentis): Uses computer vision and ML to test mobile apps the way a human user
would interact with them.
● Eggplant AI: Uses AI-driven autonomous exploration of an application to discover defects without
needing pre-written scripts.
Summary — Topic 1
AI does not replace testers; it automates the repetitive, high-volume, and maintenance-heavy parts of the
testing process. Its biggest structural innovation is self-healing automation, which allows scripts to adapt to
UI change instead of breaking. The net result for a QA team is faster releases, fewer false alarms from flaky
tests, and broader coverage achieved with the same headcount.

2. AI-Driven Test Case Generation
AI-driven test case generation refers to the use of AI and ML models to automatically read project artifacts
— requirements, user stories, defect history and UX flows — and generate relevant test cases, test data and
edge cases, without a human manually authoring every scenario from scratch.
Example: Instead of a QA engineer spending a day manually writing 40 test cases for a checkout page,
an AI model reads the associated user story and the page's navigation flow, and drafts a comparable (or
larger) set of test cases — including some edge cases a human might overlook — within minutes.
Process Overview
The process can be thought of as a simple pipeline: a set of textual and historical inputs feed into an AI
engine (typically combining Natural Language Processing with pattern-learning from past test data), which in
turn produces structured testing artifacts as outputs.
Step 1 — Inputs are collected: Requirements, user stories, past defect records, and UX/navigation flow
diagrams are gathered as the raw material the AI will read.
Step 2 — The AI engine analyses the inputs: NLP techniques extract actions, actors, and conditions from
text; pattern-learning models study relationships between past changes and past defects.
Step 3 — Outputs are generated: The engine produces test cases, associated test data, and edge cases
that a human reviewer can inspect, adjust and approve.
2.1 What AI Reads — Input Sources
● Requirements: Formal statements of expected system behaviour, e.g. "The system shall allow users to
reset their password via email." AI parses this to extract the actionable rule that needs to be tested.
● User Stories: Short descriptions of a feature from a user's perspective, e.g. "As a customer, I want to
filter products by price so I can find items in my budget." AI derives concrete filter test scenarios from
the intent expressed here.
● Past Defects: Historical bug records. If a previous defect involved a negative price crashing the price
filter, AI adds a regression test for that exact scenario so the same bug can never slip through unnoticed
again.
● UX Flow: Screen-flow or navigation diagrams (e.g. Login → Dashboard → Cart → Checkout). AI maps out
the paths a user can take through the application, ensuring test cases cover realistic navigation
sequences, not just isolated screens.
2.2 What AI Produces — Output Types
● Test Cases: Step-by-step scenarios covering functional, UI and workflow behaviour — for example,
"Verify login with valid credentials." These are typically generated with clear preconditions, steps and
expected results.

● Test Data: Realistic and varied input values generated automatically to exercise the test cases — valid
emails, invalid formats, boundary-length passwords, and so on — without a tester having to hand-craft
every value.
● Edge Cases: Rare but important scenarios that are easy for a human to overlook under time pressure —
such as a login attempt with an unusually long password, or a form submitted with every field left
empty at once.

Summary — Topic 2
AI-driven test case generation reads four kinds of inputs (requirements, user stories, past defects, UX flow)
and produces three kinds of outputs (test cases, test data, edge cases). Its single biggest benefit is surfacing
the rare edge-case scenarios that testers, under deadline pressure, are statistically most likely to miss.

Unit III — AI Techniques for Software Testing
3. ML-Based Defect Prediction
ML-based defect prediction is a machine learning approach that analyses historical code and project data to
predict which modules or files in an application are most likely to contain defects, so that limited testing
effort can be focused where it is statistically most needed.
Example: Rather than testing all 50 modules of an application with roughly equal effort, an ML model
flags the 5 modules most statistically likely to contain a defect based on past history — allowing the
team to test those modules first and in the greatest depth, within the same overall time budget.
3.1 Factors ML Analyses
● Code Complexity: Measured using metrics such as cyclomatic complexity (essentially, how many
independent decision paths a piece of code has). A function containing 15 nested if-statements is harder
for a developer to get right, and correspondingly harder to test exhaustively, than a simple linear
function.
● Previous Bugs: Modules with a history of frequent bug fixes tend to keep generating new defects. A
module that needed 12 separate bug fixes over the last year is statistically far more likely to contain the
next defect than one that has never been touched.
● Module History: Also referred to as "code churn" — how frequently a file or module has been modified,
and by how many different developers. A file edited by 8 different developers within a single month
signals architectural instability and a higher chance of integration defects.
3.2 The Defect Prediction Pipeline
Turning raw historical project data into an actionable risk score for each module follows a five-stage pipeline:
Step 1 — Collect Historical Data: Source-control commit history, defect-tracking records and code
metrics are gathered across the codebase, typically over the last several months or years.
Step 2 — Extract Features: Numerical features are computed for each module — e.g. cyclomatic
complexity, historical bug count, and change frequency (churn).
Step 3 — Train the ML Model: A supervised learning algorithm (commonly a Random Forest or Logistic
Regression model) is trained on the historical features, learning the relationship between these metrics
and where defects actually occurred in the past.
Step 4 — Predict Defect-Prone Modules: The trained model scores every current module, producing a
risk classification (e.g. High / Medium / Low) for each one.
Step 5 — Prioritize and Allocate Test Effort: Testers use the risk scores to decide where to invest deep
exploratory and regression testing, and where lighter smoke testing is sufficient.
3.3 Worked Example — Module Risk Scoring
Consider an ML model trained on 12 months of commit and defect history for an e-commerce application. It
might produce the following risk assessment:

Summary — Topic 3
ML-based defect prediction combines three inputs — code complexity, previous bugs and module change
history — to train a model that scores each module's likelihood of containing a defect. The outcome is a
smarter allocation of limited testing time: more depth where the data says it matters, less where it doesn't.

4. AI in Requirement Analysis (NLP)
Natural Language Processing (NLP) refers to a family of AI techniques that allow software to read and
interpret plain-English text. Applied to requirement analysis, NLP reads requirement documents, user stories
and acceptance criteria, extracts structured meaning from them, and uses that understanding both to
generate test cases and to flag quality issues in the requirements themselves — before a single line of code
is written.
Example: A 40-page Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document that would take a tester a full
day to review manually can be scanned by an NLP engine in a matter of minutes to extract every testable
rule it contains.
Process Overview
Conceptually, this too follows an inputs → engine → outputs pattern, but the engine here is specifically an
NLP pipeline rather than a general ML model:
Step 1 — Input requirement text is collected: Requirement documents, user stories, and acceptance
criteria are gathered as plain-text input.
Step 2 — NLP parses and extracts meaning: The engine identifies actors ("who"), actions ("what"), and
conditions ("under what circumstance") within each requirement sentence, and separately checks the text
for vague or unmeasurable language.
Step 3 — Structured outputs are produced: Draft test cases, ambiguity flags, and automatically compiled
test reports are generated for the QA and business-analysis teams to review.
4.1 Core Capabilities
i. Converts Requirement Documents into Test Cases
NLP identifies the actor, action and condition embedded in a requirement sentence, and uses this structure
to draft a corresponding test case automatically.
Example: Requirement: "The system shall lock the account after 3 failed login attempts." From this single
sentence, NLP auto-generates a test case that verifies the account is indeed locked precisely on the 3rd
failed attempt — not the 2nd, and not the 4th.
ii. Identifies Missing or Ambiguous Requirements
Many requirements are written with vague, unmeasurable language that different readers could interpret
differently. NLP can detect such wording and flag it for clarification before it causes a defect downstream.
Example: Requirement: "The system should respond quickly." This is flagged as ambiguous, because
"quickly" has no measurable threshold. NLP prompts the team to define an exact figure — for example,
"the system shall respond within 2 seconds" — before development begins.
iii. Auto-Generates Test Reports

flagged risk areas — into a shareable report, removing the manual spreadsheet work traditionally required

Summary — Topic 4
NLP-based requirement analysis effectively shifts testing left — ambiguities are caught at the requirement

The four topics in this unit together describe how AI supports software testing across the full lifecycle —

Topic Core Idea
1. Why AI in Testing AI reduces manual effort in high-volume, change-heavy, maintenance-heavy
testing tasks while improving speed, accuracy and coverage.
2. Test Case Generation AI reads requirements, user stories, defects and UX flow to auto-produce test

3. Defect Prediction ML analyses code complexity, bug history and module change history to
predict and prioritize defect-prone modules.
4. Requirement Analysis (NLP) NLP converts requirement text into test cases, flags ambiguous or missing

UNIT I: Introduction to Cloud Computing (6 Hours)

1. Evolution and History of Cloud Computing Cloud computing did not appear suddenly – it evolved through several stages of computing technology: • Mainframe Computing (1950s–60s): Large, centralized computers shared by many users via "dumb terminals. " Expensive and centrally managed – the root idea of "shared computing resources. " • Client-Server Computing (1980s–90s): Personal computers (clients) connected to central servers. Gave users more control but reduced central resource sharing. • Grid Computing (1990s): Multiple computers linked together to work as one powerful system on a shared task – introduced the idea of pooling distributed resources. • Utility Computing (2000s): Computing resources offered as a metered, pay-per-use service, like electricity or water – this is the direct ancestor of cloud billing. • Cloud Computing (2006 onwards): Combines virtualization, utility computing, grid computing, and web services. Amazon Web Services (AWS) launched EC2 and S3 in 2006, which is generally considered the formal start of modern cloud computing. Easy way to remember: Mainframe → Client-Server → Grid → Utility → Cloud (resources moved from "centralized" → "distributed" → "on-demand, pay-per-use, anywhere access"). 2. Introduction to Cloud Computing Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services – servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics – over the Internet ("the cloud"), instead of owning and maintaining physical hardware. Simple definition: "Using someone else's computers (servers), over the internet, and paying only for what " you use. NIST Definition (commonly asked): Definition: Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (networks, servers, storage, applications, services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction. 3. Why Cloud Computing is Becoming Highly Important • Businesses avoid huge upfront investment in hardware (capital expenditure → operational expenditure). • Enables remote work and global collaboration – access data/apps from anywhere. • Supports rapid scaling – companies can grow or shrink IT resources instantly based on demand (e.g., e-commerce sites during sales). • Reduces the burden of maintenance, upgrades, and IT staff for individual businesses. • Encourages innovation – startups can launch products quickly without building data centers. • Supports big data, AI, and IoT applications that need massive, flexible computing power. 4. Features of Cloud Computing Feature Meaning On-Demand Self-Service Users can provision resources (storage, servers) automatically w Broad Network Access Services available over the internet, accessible from any device (la Resource Pooling Provider's resources are pooled to serve multiple customers (multi- Rapid Elasticity Resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.

Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 3 Feature Meaning Measured Service Usage is monitored and billed on a pay-per-use basis (like an elec Multi-Tenancy Multiple users/organizations share the same physical infrastructur 5. Cloud Computing for Various Users • Individual users: Email (Gmail), storage (Google Drive, Dropbox), streaming (Netflix, Spotify). • Small businesses: Website hosting, accounting software (SaaS tools) without owning servers. • Large enterprises: Big data analytics, disaster recovery, global app deployment. • Developers: Platforms (PaaS) to build, test, and deploy applications without managing infrastructure. • Government/Education: Cost-effective large-scale data storage and e-governance services. 6. Advantages of Cloud Computing • Cost savings – no need to buy/maintain physical hardware; pay-as-you-go. • Scalability & flexibility – easily scale resources up/down. • Accessibility – access from anywhere with internet. • Automatic updates – provider handles maintenance and software updates. • Disaster recovery & backup – data replicated across multiple locations. • Faster deployment – new applications/services can be launched quickly. • Collaboration – teams can work on shared documents/projects in real time. 7. Limitations of Cloud Computing • Internet dependency – no internet means no access to cloud services. • Security & privacy concerns – sensitive data is stored on third-party servers. • Limited control – customers don't have full control over the underlying infrastructure. • Downtime risk – if the provider's servers fail, users are affected. • Vendor lock-in – difficult/costly to migrate from one cloud provider to another. • Ongoing costs – long-term subscription costs may exceed one-time hardware purchase in some cases.
