Layers and Types of Cloud The cloud architecture is typically layered: Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 5 • Infrastructure Layer (physical servers, storage, networking – base layer) • Platform Layer (OS, runtime environments, development tools) • Application Layer (end-user software/applications, topmost layer) 6. Components of Cloud Computing • Clients – devices (desktops, laptops, mobiles) used to access cloud services. • Datacenters – collection of servers that host applications and store data. • Distributed Servers – servers located in different geographic locations for redundancy and fast access. • Cloud-based Delivery (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS) – the services offered. 7. Cloud Computing Service Providers Major players offering cloud services: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform

(GCP), IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud, Salesforce.
8. Software as a Service (SaaS)
Definition: A software distribution model where applications are hosted by a provider and made available
to customers over the internet, typically through a web browser – no installation needed.
9. Evolution of SaaS
• Started with Application Service Providers (ASPs) in the late 1990s, who hosted software for businesses.
• Evolved with the growth of the internet and web technologies into modern multi-tenant SaaS applications (e.g.,
Salesforce, launched in 1999, is considered a SaaS pioneer).
• Broadband growth, virtualization, and web 2.0 accelerated SaaS adoption in the 2000s–2010s.
10. SaaS Unification Technologies
Technologies/approaches that help combine (unify) data and functionality from multiple SaaS applications so they
work together seamlessly, such as APIs, middleware, and integration platforms.
11. SaaS Integration Products and Technologies
Tools used to connect SaaS applications with each other or with on-premises systems:
• API-based integration (most common)
• Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)
• iPaaS (Integration Platform as a Service) – e.g., MuleSoft, Dell Boomi, Zapier
12. SaaS Product Selection Criteria
When choosing a SaaS product, organizations evaluate:
• Functionality – does it meet business requirements?
• Security & compliance – data protection standards.
• Integration capability – can it connect with existing systems?
• Scalability – can it grow with the business?
• Cost – subscription pricing vs. value delivered.
• Vendor reliability – uptime guarantees (SLA), support quality.
• Customization – flexibility to adapt to specific workflows.
Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 6
13. SaaS Integration Services
Professional/managed services that help businesses connect their SaaS applications with other systems
(data migration, workflow automation, API management) – often provided by third-party integration specialists
or the SaaS vendor itself.
14. Advantages of SaaS
• No installation or maintenance needed by the user.
• Accessible from any device with a browser and internet.
• Automatic updates and patches handled by the vendor.
• Lower upfront cost – subscription-based pricing.
• Easy scalability – add/remove users as needed.
• Faster deployment compared to traditional software.

Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 7
UNIT III: Platform as a Service (PaaS) (6 Hours)
1. Introduction to PaaS
PaaS provides a complete development and deployment environment in the cloud – including servers,
storage, OS, and middleware – so developers can build, test, and deploy applications without managing the
underlying infrastructure.
Simple definition: "A ready-made platform where developers just write code – everything else (servers,
OS, database engine) is managed by the provider.
"
2. Evolution of PaaS
• Emerged as an extension of IaaS once developers wanted to focus purely on coding, not infrastructure setup.
• Early PaaS offerings (mid-2000s) like Google App Engine (2008) and Force.com (Salesforce's platform) allowed
developers to build apps without provisioning servers.

• Modern PaaS supports multiple languages, frameworks, containers, and microservices architectures. 3. PaaS Service Providers Provider Description Acquia Cloud PaaS specifically built for hosting and managing Drupal-base website Amazon AWS (Elastic Beanstalk) AWS's PaaS offering – automatically handles deployment, capacity Google App Engine Fully managed platform for building and deploying scalable web app Force.com Salesforce's PaaS for building business applications on top of the S 4. Amazon Elastic Beanstalk (detail) • A PaaS from AWS that automates deployment: developer uploads code, and Beanstalk manages the deployment, capacity provisioning, load balancing, auto-scaling, and application health monitoring. • Supports multiple languages: Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go. • Developer still has access to underlying AWS resources if needed (more flexible than pure PaaS). 5. Google App Engine (detail) • Fully managed serverless platform. • Automatically scales applications up/down based on traffic. • Supports standard environment (sandboxed, specific languages) and flexible environment (custom Docker containers). • No server management required at all. 6. Force.com (detail) • Platform provided by Salesforce for building custom business applications. • Uses Apex (proprietary programming language) and Visualforce for UI development. • Deep integration with Salesforce CRM data and workflows. 7. PaaS Application Framework A set of pre-built tools, libraries, and components that provide a foundation for building applications on the PaaS – includes: • Programming language support (Java, Python, Ruby, etc.) Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 8 • Database management tools • Built-in APIs for common functionality (authentication, messaging) • Application lifecycle management (build, test, deploy) 8. PaaS Operator Verbs

Actions performed by the operator/administrator managing the PaaS platform itself:
• Provision – allocate resources.
• Manage/Monitor – track platform health and performance.
• Migrate – move applications/data between environments.
• Secure – configure access controls and security policies.
9. PaaS Developer Verbs
Actions performed by developers using the PaaS to build applications:
• Develop/Build – write application code.
• Deploy – publish the application to the platform.
• Test/Debug – verify application functionality.
• Scale – configure how the application should handle varying load (often automated).
(Easy way to differentiate: Operator Verbs = platform-level actions by admins; Developer Verbs = application-level
actions by coders.)
10. Advantages of PaaS
• Faster development – developers focus only on code, not infrastructure.
• Reduced coding time using pre-built frameworks and tools.
• Automatic scalability and load balancing.
• Supports collaborative development (multiple developers working simultaneously).
• Lower cost – no need to buy/manage servers or OS licenses.
• Simplified deployment process.
11. Challenges of PaaS
• Vendor lock-in – applications built on one PaaS may not easily migrate to another.
• Limited control over underlying infrastructure and configurations.
• Runtime/language restrictions – must use supported languages/frameworks.
• Security concerns – dependent on provider's security practices.
• Integration issues with legacy/on-premises systems.
Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 9
UNIT IV: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and
Cloud Data (6 Hours)
Part A: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
1. Introduction & Evolution of IaaS

IaaS provides virtualized computing resources over the internet – virtual machines, storage, networks
– allowing customers to rent infrastructure instead of buying physical hardware.
• Evolved from traditional data center hosting/colocation services, combined with virtualization technology,
which allowed a single physical server to be divided into multiple virtual servers.
• Amazon EC2 (2006) is widely considered the pioneer of modern IaaS.
Simple definition: "Renting virtual computers (servers), storage, and networking on-demand, paying only for
what is used – like renting an empty apartment where you bring your own furniture (OS and software).
"
2. IaaS Architecture
Key layers in IaaS architecture:
• Physical Hardware Layer – actual servers, storage devices, network hardware in the data center.
• Virtualization Layer (Hypervisor) – software that creates and manages virtual machines (VMs) on top of
physical hardware.
• Virtual Resource Layer – the VMs, virtual storage, and virtual networks that customers actually use.
• Management/Orchestration Layer – tools for provisioning, monitoring, scaling, and billing resources.
•
User Access Layer – APIs, dashboards, and CLI tools customers use to manage their infrastructure. 3.
SAN Model (Storage Area Network)
• A SAN is a dedicated high-speed network that provides block-level network access to storage, separate from
the regular local area network (LAN).
• Used in IaaS to give servers fast, reliable, and scalable access to shared storage resources.
•
Improves storage utilization, enables centralized storage management, and supports disaster recovery. 4.
IaaS Providers
Major IaaS providers: Amazon Web Services (AWS EC2), Microsoft Azure, Google Compute Engine, IBM
Cloud, Rackspace, DigitalOcean.
5. Advantages of IaaS
• Cost-efficient – no capital expenditure on physical hardware.
• Scalability – resources scale up/down instantly based on demand.
• Flexibility – full control over OS, storage, and installed applications.
• Faster provisioning – new servers can be deployed within minutes.
• Disaster recovery – easier backup and replication across regions.
• Reduced maintenance burden – provider maintains the physical hardware.
6. Disadvantages of IaaS
• Security responsibility shared – customer must still secure OS/applications (shared responsibility model).
Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 10
• Requires technical expertise to manage servers, OS, and networking.
• Ongoing operational costs can add up over long-term usage.
• Potential downtime if the provider experiences outages.
• Dependency on internet connectivity.

Part B: Data in Cloud
7. Evolution of Network Storage in Cloud
• Traditional storage: Direct Attached Storage (DAS) – storage physically attached to a single server.
• Evolved to Network Attached Storage (NAS) – storage accessible over a network by multiple users.
• Further evolved to Storage Area Networks (SAN) – dedicated high-speed storage networks.
• Cloud storage represents the latest evolution: virtualized, distributed, and globally accessible storage
delivered as a service over the internet.
8. Data as a Service (DaaS)
• A service model where data (not software or infrastructure) is provided on-demand to users, regardless of their
location, through the cloud.
• Enables organizations to access high-quality, up-to-date data without managing the underlying data infrastructure.
• Example: Financial market data feeds delivered via cloud APIs.
9. Database as a Service (DBaaS)
• A cloud service that provides access to a database without the need to set up physical hardware, install
software, or manage the database configuration.
• Provider handles maintenance, backups, patching, and scaling.
• Examples: Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Azure SQL Database.
10. Cloud Based Data Storage
Storage services where data is stored on remote servers accessed via the internet, managed by a cloud provider:
• Object Storage – for unstructured data (e.g., Amazon S3).
• Block Storage – for structured data needing high performance (e.g., Amazon EBS).
• File Storage – for shared file systems accessible by multiple instances (e.g., Amazon EFS).
11. Advantages of Cloud-Based Storage
• Accessible from anywhere with an internet connection.
• Automatic backup and data redundancy across locations.
• Highly scalable – pay only for storage used.
• Easy sharing and collaboration on files.
• Reduced hardware maintenance costs.
12. Limitations of Cloud-Based Storage Solutions
• Dependent on internet connectivity for access.
• Security and privacy risks (data stored off-premises).
• Potential latency issues for very large files.
Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 11
• Ongoing subscription costs.
• Data transfer/egress fees when moving large amounts of data out of the
cloud. 13. Cloud-Based Data Storage Service Providers
Examples: Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, Dropbox, Box.

Fundamentals of Cloud Computing – SYBCA Semester III Page 12
UNIT V: Virtualization (6 Hours)
1. Introduction to Virtualization
Virtualization is the technology that allows creation of a virtual (rather than physical) version of something –
such as a server, storage device, network, or operating system – enabling multiple virtual systems to run on a
single physical machine.

Simple definition: "Dividing one physical computer into multiple 'pretend' computers, each behaving like an independent machine. " Virtualization is the foundation technology that makes cloud computing possible – it allows cloud providers to share physical hardware among many customers safely and efficiently. 2. Technical Evolution and History of Virtualization • 1960s: IBM introduced virtualization concepts on mainframes (CP/CMS system) to allow multiple users to share expensive mainframe hardware. • 1990s–2000s: x86 virtualization became practical with software like VMware, enabling virtualization on standard desktop/server hardware. • 2000s–present: Virtualization became central to cloud computing, enabling providers like AWS and Azure to offer virtual machines to millions of customers on shared physical infrastructure. 3. Types of Virtual Machines Type Description System Virtual Machine Provides a complete virtual environment that can run a full operating Process Virtual Machine (Application VM) Runs a single program/process in a platform-independent environm 4. Advantages of Virtualization • Better hardware utilization – multiple VMs run on one physical server, reducing waste. • Cost savings – fewer physical machines needed, reducing hardware and energy costs. • Isolation – a problem in one VM doesn't affect others on the same host. • Easy backup and disaster recovery – VMs can be easily copied, backed up, or moved. • Scalability – new VMs can be created quickly to meet demand. • Testing and development flexibility – developers can create isolated test environments easily. 5. Components of Virtualization • Host Machine – the physical computer on which virtualization takes place. • Hypervisor (Virtual Machine Monitor - VMM) – software layer that creates and manages virtual machines, allocating physical resources (CPU, memory, storage) to each VM. • Guest Machine (Virtual Machine) – the virtual system running on top of the host, behaving like an independent computer. • Virtual Hardware – the virtualized CPU, memory, storage, and network interfaces presented to each guest VM. 6. Types of Virtualization Type Description Example Hardware/Server Virtualization Creating multiple virtual servers on one phy hypervisor.
